name: 'Existence' as bad syntax (the critique of predicating existence of things)
plain_explanation: It is nonsense to say of a particular thing, pointed to directly, that 'this exists'; we can only sensibly say that a description ('the largest lion in the Zoo') applies to something, i.e. that there is an x satisfying it.
precise_definition: Russell's argument that 'exists' is a predicate applicable only to descriptions (incomplete or complete), not to names or to bare percepts; 'lions exist' means 'there are lions,' i.e. "'x is a lion' is true for a suitable x," and one cannot coherently add, of a perceived particular, 'and that exists.'
why_it_mattered: It dismantles Plato's claim that the mind directly apprehends 'existence' as a special object alongside sound and colour, and it also undercuts the ontological argument for the existence of God, which trades on the same confusion.
historical_origin: Russell's own logical analysis, developed in this chapter as a response to Plato's argument in the Theaetetus.
examples: Taking a child to the zoo and saying 'look, that's a lion' proves lions exist without needing to add 'and you can see that that exists'
competing_positions: Plato's view that 'existence,' like likeness and number, is among the things the mind apprehends by itself, without any sense-organ
influence_on_later_thinkers: Directly relevant, Russell notes, 'to other matters such as the ontological argument for the existence of the Deity.'
